etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English animal, from Old French animal, from Latin animal, a nominal use of an adjective from animale, neuter of animālis, from anima (“breath, spirit”). Displaced native Middle English deor, der (“animal”) (whence modern English deer; from Old English dēor (“animal”)), Middle English reother (“animal, neat”) (whence modern English rother; from Old English hrīþer, hrȳþer (“neat, ox”)).

definitions.definition: (sciences) Any eukaryote of the clade Animalia; a  multicellular organism that is usually mobile, whose cells are not encased in a rigid cell wall (distinguishing it from plants and fungi) and which derives energy solely from the consumption of other organisms (distinguishing it from plants).

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, “Of the Cameleon”, in Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC, 3rd book, page 133:
quote.text: It cannot be denied it [the chameleon] is (if not the moſt of any) a very abſtemious animall, and ſuch as by reaſon of its frigidity, paucity of bloud, and latitancy in the winter (about which time the obſervations are often made) will long ſubſist without a viſible ſuſtentation.

definitions.definition: (loosely) Any member of the kingdom Animalia other than a human.
(colloquial) A tetrapod; a land-dwelling nonhuman vertebrate.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Henry Petroski, “Geothermal Energy”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 4:

definitions.definition: A warm-blooded animal; a mammal or bird.

definitions.definition: (loosely) A higher animal; an animal related to humans.
(figuratively) A person who behaves wildly; a bestial, brutal, brutish, cruel, or inhuman person.

definitions.definition: (informal) A person of a particular type specified by an adjective.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English animal, from Latin animālis, from either anima (“breath, spirit”) or animus. Originally distinct from the noun, it became associated with attributive use of the noun and is now indistinguishable from it.
